extracted.intended_audience: poets, poetry students, teachers, and readers seeking a concise definition and rules for the villanelle form
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing the fixed poetic form villanelle: stanza count and line-repetition pattern that define the form, with canonical examples cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stanza structure (five tercets + final quatrain)
rubrics_metrics.description: A French verse form consisting of five three-line stanzas and a final quatrain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The villanelle is built from five tercets (three-line stanzas) followed by a final four-line stanza (quatrain). Examples cited on the page include Dylan Thomas's “Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night,” Elizabeth Bishop’s “One Art,” and Edwin Arlington Robinson’s “The House on the Hill.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain and line-repetition pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and third lines of the first stanza repeat alternately in the following stanzas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those two refrain lines (the repeated first and third lines from stanza one) alternate as the closing lines of subsequent tercets and then form the final couplet in the quatrain. This alternating-refrain pattern is the defining characteristic that creates the villanelle's circular, echoing effect.
